message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"d625caa0f65592ba54088e350f8e69f122739225de2104c7168d473bf117c3a1","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-ny-class-d:lineage:62","source_registry_sha256":"f5f0e765d8ae90e6aae6e6bbb4e1e1ba64f643ffc8ff14436ec954958fb7f36d","units":[{"unit_id":"sec05-u01","module_id":"sec05-m01","objective_ids":["sec05-u01"],"title":{"text":"Who goes first at intersections","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Most crashes strike at intersections and in big parking lots during turns.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Right-of-way rules settle the conflicts that signs and green lights leave open.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F04"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Ben has a green light to go straight, and a left turner is already in the middle of the intersection.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Approaching drivers yield to traffic already inside, even on a green.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]},"result":{"text":"Ben waits for the left turner to finish, then enters.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a green light means you never have to wait for anyone.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]},"correction":{"text":"A green-straight driver still waits out a left turner who is already in the intersection.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Inside first, straight before left, right beats left.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Two cars reach an uncontrolled right-angle corner at the same moment, both going straight. Which one gives way?","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},"answer":{"text":"The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},"rationale":{"text":"At uncontrolled or simultaneous-stop right-angle corners the left driver yields, even straight against straight.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Sorting out who goes first","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Most crashes happen during turns.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Rules for who yields.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson opens the chapter on intersections and turns. The manual starts with a sobering point: most crashes strike at intersections and in big parking lots while drivers are turning. Signs and green lights do not settle every conflict, such as a left turner facing traffic coming straight through. That is the job of right-of-way rules. We will cover three of them: yielding to traffic already inside the intersection, the priority of straight and right movements over left turns, and the rule for two drivers meeting at a right-angle corner. Then we will see why the left side keeps losing.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Traffic already inside","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Approaching drivers yield to those inside.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Even on a green light.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Wait out the left turner.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"The first rule is about timing. Drivers approaching an intersection yield to traffic that is already inside it. So if you have a green light to go straight, and a left turner is already in the middle of the intersection, you wait for that driver to finish before you enter. Your green light does not outrank a driver who got there first and is still in the box. The manual gives exactly this example: a green-straight driver waits out a left turner who is already mid-intersection. Hold it as the base rule for every intersection: whoever is already inside goes first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Straight before left","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Opposite arrivals: straight and right first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Left turner enters, right of center.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Finish when oncoming clears.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Now suppose two drivers arrive at the same time from opposite directions. Straight and right movements get priority over left turns. A left turner may enter on green only when nobody ahead is also turning left, and waits there holding right of center with the wheels straight. The turn is finished once oncoming traffic clears. The same yielding applies when turning left into a driveway or parking lot. And if a gap looks doubtful, the manual says to wait it out. So the left turner is the one who waits, and waits patiently, until the way is truly clear.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Right-angle corners","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"No control, or both stop at once.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Left driver yields to right driver.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Even straight against straight.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"The third rule covers right-angle intersections. When a corner has no signs or signals, or when two drivers stop at the same moment, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. This holds even when both drivers are going straight. So the question at such a corner is not who is turning, but who is on whose right. If the other car is on your right, you yield. If you are on the other driver's right, the other driver yields to you. Learn to glance at the cross street and ask that single question each time you arrive at an uncontrolled corner.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Why the left side loses","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Opposite arrivals: left turners yield.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Right-angle corners: left driver yields.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Two rules, different reasons.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Two of these rules both make the left side lose, but for different reasons, and people mix them up. At opposite arrivals, a left turn bows to straight and right traffic, because of the movement it is making. At simultaneous-stop or uncontrolled right-angle corners, the left driver bows to the right driver, because of where the two cars sit. So leftness loses in both geometries. If a question describes cars meeting head-on with one turning left, think movement. If it describes cars meeting at a right angle, think position, and the car on the right goes first.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the right-angle rule","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two cars, right angle, both straight.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01"]},{"text":"Who gives way?","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: two cars reach an uncontrolled right-angle corner at the same moment, and both drivers plan to go straight. Which one gives way? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the driver on the left, who yields to the driver on the right. That holds even though both are going straight, because at right-angle corners the rule is about position. If you were thinking about left turns, that rule is for drivers arriving from opposite directions, where straight and right movements go before a left turn. Two rules, and in both the left side loses.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Right-of-way in short","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Inside first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Straight and right before left.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Right beats left at corners.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, most crashes strike at intersections and in big parking lots during turns, and right-of-way rules settle what signs and greens leave open. Drivers approaching an intersection yield to traffic already inside. When drivers arrive from opposite directions together, straight and right movements go before left turns, and a left turner waits right of center with straight wheels until oncoming traffic clears. At uncontrolled or simultaneous-stop right-angle corners, the left driver yields to the right driver, even straight against straight. Next we leave driveways, meet pedestrians and keep intersections clear.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u02","module_id":"sec05-m02","objective_ids":["sec05-u02"],"title":{"text":"Driveways, pedestrians and full intersections","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02","sec05-F06"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Leaving a driveway, lot or private road means stopping and yielding to road traffic and pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Pedestrians in crosswalks, marked or not, get the right-of-way.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Lena's light turns green, but traffic is backed up on the far side of the intersection.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Never enter on a green you cannot clear; wait out a backed-up far side instead of gridlocking the box.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"result":{"text":"Lena waits behind the line until there is room on the far side.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a green light means you should pull into the intersection even if traffic ahead is stopped.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"correction":{"text":"Never enter on a green you cannot clear; wait out backed-up far sides instead of gridlocking the box.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Driveway: stop for all. Crosswalk: walkers first. Box: clear it or wait.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You are leaving a parking lot and will turn left onto the road. Which ways must you watch?","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},"answer":{"text":"Both ways for traffic, and for any crossing pedestrian.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},"rationale":{"text":"Lot exits stop and yield, watching left for right exits and both ways for left exits.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Edges of the intersection","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driveways, lots and private roads.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Crosswalks, full boxes and circles.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the places where drivers join traffic or share it with people on foot. We start with leaving driveways, parking lots and private roads, where the rule is to stop and yield. Then we compare that with entering an intersection on a green light, which works very differently. After that we turn to pedestrians in crosswalks, marked or not, and to the rule against entering an intersection you cannot clear. We finish with traffic circles and rotaries, where entering drivers yield to those already going around. Each rule answers the same question in a new place: who goes first here?","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Leaving a driveway or lot","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop and yield to traffic and pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Right exit: watch left.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Left exit: watch both ways.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"When you leave a driveway, a parking lot, or a private road, you must stop and yield to traffic on the roadway and to pedestrians. Where you look depends on where you are going. For a right exit, watch to the left. For a left exit, watch both ways. And in every case, watch for any pedestrian crossing in front of you. So the exit rule has three parts: stop, yield to road traffic and people, and look in the directions your turn requires before you pull out. The same stop-and-yield rule covers all three kinds of exit: driveways, parking lots and private roads. Stop first, then yield, then look the way your turn needs.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Driveway versus green light","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F02","sec05-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driveway exit: stop for everything.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F02","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Green entry: yield only to those inside.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F02","sec05-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. People sometimes carry the driveway rule into intersections, or the green-light rule into driveways. The manual sets them side by side. Driveway exits stop for everything. Green lights stop for nobody except whoever is already inside the intersection. One is entry caution, and the other is earned passage. So when you leave a lot, you stop and give way to all road traffic and pedestrians. When you have a green at an intersection, you go, unless someone is already inside, in which case you wait for them. Keep each rule in its own place.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F02","sec05-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pedestrians in crosswalks","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yield in crosswalks, marked or not.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},{"text":"Slow or stop; guard cyclists too.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},{"text":"Wait out red-light crossers after green.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Drivers yield to pedestrians who are lawfully in a crosswalk, whether the crosswalk is marked or not. Slow down or stop as needed, and guard cyclists too. When your light turns green, a pedestrian who started crossing on the red may still be in the street, and you wait them out. Before you turn, wait for crosswalk users on either side of you. So the green light does not clear the crosswalk for you. People already walking finish first. Watch the crosswalk you are about to cross, on the side you are turning toward and on the side you are coming from.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Clear the box or wait","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Never enter on a green you cannot clear.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},{"text":"Watch backed-up far sides.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},{"text":"Watch offset cross-streets.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Never enter an intersection on a green light if you cannot clear it. If the far side is backed up, or an offset cross-street means traffic beyond is stopped, wait behind the line instead. Entering and stopping in the middle is what the manual calls gridlocking the box. The manual's rule is simple: you need room on the far side before you go in. So look past the intersection, not only at your signal, and ask whether there is space for your car on the other side. If there is not, the green light is not yet yours to use, and you hold your place.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Circles and rotaries","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Entrants yield to circulating traffic.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Roundabout technique comes later.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Traffic circles and rotaries follow one clear rule for entering. Drivers entering a circle or rotary yield to everyone already circulating. So you wait for a gap in the traffic going around, and you merge in when it is safe. The vehicles already in the circle do not have to stop for you. The manual notes that the technique for roundabouts is covered in more detail in the defensive driving chapter, so this lesson keeps to the yielding rule. Think of it as another form of the base rule from the last lesson: traffic already inside, whether in an intersection or a circle, goes first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the lot exit","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Leaving a lot, turning left.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"Which ways do you watch?","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are leaving a parking lot and you plan to turn left onto the road. Which ways must you watch? Work it out before reading on. The answer is both ways for road traffic, and for any crossing pedestrian, after you stop and yield. The manual says left exits watch both ways. If you were turning right, the rule would have you watch to the left. And unlike entering an intersection on green, a driveway or lot exit stops for everything, not just for drivers already inside. So for this left exit you stop, yield to road traffic and pedestrians, and look both ways before you pull out.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Yielding at the edges","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driveway exits: stop and yield.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Crosswalk walkers come first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Clear the box; yield in circles.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, driveway, lot and private-road exits must stop and yield to roadway traffic and pedestrians, watching left for right exits, both ways for left exits, and for any crossing pedestrian. Driveway exits stop for everything, while green lights stop for nobody except whoever is already inside. Yield to lawful crosswalk pedestrians, marked or not, wait out red-light crossers after green, and guard cyclists. Never enter on a green you cannot clear. And when entering a circle or rotary, yield to everyone already circulating. Next we look at emergency vehicles and the Move Over law.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-R02","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u03","module_id":"sec05-m03","objective_ids":["sec05-u03"],"title":{"text":"Emergency vehicles and Move Over","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Red flashes on fire, ambulance and police vehicles command an immediate pull to the right and stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},{"text":"The Move Over law protects vehicles stopped on the shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Raj is on an interstate and sees a car stopped on the shoulder ahead with amber lights flashing.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]},"reasoning":{"text":"The Move Over law demands care, reduced speed and a lane shift away from shoulder-stopped vehicles flashing amber, unless unsafe.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]},"result":{"text":"Raj slows down and moves one lane away as he passes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you must pull over for any vehicle with a flashing light.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},"correction":{"text":"Blue, green and amber displayers are not authorized emergency vehicles; others yield to them only by courtesy.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-R03"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Red, pull over; blue, green, amber, courtesy; shoulder, move over.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A car with a flashing blue light approaches from behind. Must you pull over?","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},"answer":{"text":"No, blue marks a volunteer firefighter, and yielding is a courtesy.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},"rationale":{"text":"Only red, red-blue or red-white flashes command a pull-over stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F09"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Lights, sirens and the shoulder","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red flashes command a stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12"]},{"text":"Other colors and the Move Over law.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about vehicles with flashing lights. The manual separates three situations. First, authorized emergency vehicles with red flashing lights, which command you to pull over and stop. Second, what those responders are allowed to do, which is why you stay extra cautious around them. Third, the Move Over law, which protects vehicles stopped on the shoulder. And finally, vehicles with blue, green or amber lights, which are not authorized emergency vehicles at all. Telling these apart is the core of the lesson, because each one asks something different of you as a driver.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pull right and stop","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red, red-blue or red-white flashes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},{"text":"Pull safely to the right edge and stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},{"text":"From every direction, after clearing the intersection.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Fire trucks, ambulances, police and other authorized emergency responders show red, red-blue or red-white flashing lights, and may also use sirens or air horns, though police may skip the siren. When one approaches, you must pull safely to the right edge of the road and stop, immediately. That applies from every direction, including when the vehicle is coming toward you in the opposite lane of a two-way road, and even when you hear a siren but cannot tell where it is. If you are in an intersection, clear it first, then pull right and stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What responders may do","fact_ids":["sec05-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Speed, run reds and stop signs.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10"]},{"text":"Reverse one-way streets, invent turns.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10"]},{"text":"Stay extra cautious.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"An emergency driver with lights on and siren sounding may legally do things you may not. They may speed, run red lights and stop or yield signs, go the wrong way on one-way streets, and make turning moves that are normally not allowed. The responder still has a duty of care, but drivers nearby stay extra cautious because of these privileges. So when you see or hear one, do not assume it will follow the usual rules of the road. Pull over as required, and stay alert around it. The privileges are speeding, running red lights and stop or yield signs, reversing one-way streets and inventing turning moves, all legal for a lit and sounding responder.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The Move Over law","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Care and reduced speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]},{"text":"Lane shift on multilane highways.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]},{"text":"A moving violation if ignored.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"The Move Over law protects vehicles stopped on the shoulder. When you approach an emergency or hazard vehicle stopped on the shoulder with emergency, amber or blue-green lights flashing, use care and reduce your speed. On multilane parkways, interstates and controlled highways, also shift into a lane away from it, unless that is unsafe. The law also covers vehicles with blue-green lights and any vehicle parked on the shoulder of a parkway or controlled highway. Breaking the Move Over law is punishable as a moving violation, so treat it as a firm duty, not a suggestion.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Blue, green and amber","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Blue: volunteer firefighters.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},{"text":"Green: volunteer ambulance crews.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},{"text":"Amber: plows, tow rigs, mail, buses.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Some vehicles flash colors other than red. Volunteer firefighters show blue lights. Volunteer ambulance crews show green. Snowplows, tow rigs, tow vehicles with blue combinations, rural mail carriers and school buses show amber. None of these count as authorized emergency vehicles. Their drivers must obey every traffic law, and other drivers yield to them only as a courtesy. So a blue or green light behind you does not create the same duty as a red one. You may let them by as a courtesy, but the command to pull over and stop belongs to red flashes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Command, courtesy, shoulder","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F09","sec05-F11","sec05-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red flashes: pull over and stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F09","sec05-F11","sec05-F12"]},{"text":"Blue, green, amber: courtesy only.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F09","sec05-F11","sec05-F12"]},{"text":"Move Over: every stopped shoulder vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F09","sec05-F11","sec05-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Because all of these vehicles flash lights, people treat every light the same. The manual sorts them into three duties. Red-flashing responders command pull-over stops.
